answer: The submission is honest and clearly written, but it reads as a well-framed idea rather than an evidence-backed venture. Priority improvements: (1) Quantify the problem and market. Replace 'several million' and 'a meaningful portion' with cited figures (e.g., number of 18-34 adults with chronic conditions, % reporting cost-related nonadherence), then build a bottom-up TAM/SAM/SOM and a realistic beachhead (campus population x chronic-condition prevalence x expected adoption). (2) Present traction with numbers. State how many pilot users, how many sessions, which medications were compared, any early savings examples (e.g., 'user X saved $Y on drug Z'), and 2-3 short user quotes. 'Early comments suggest' is too vague; even a small, measured set of metrics (savings per fill, repeat usage after 30 days) would raise credibility. (3) Build a simple financial model. Show assumptions for referral fee per fill, fills per user per month, free-to-paid conversion, CAC, and cost of data licensing, then break-even user counts and a line-item use of the $75K by month/milestone. Currently the revenue case rests on unsigned agreements and unknown conversion. (4) Sharpen the competitive differentiation. Name specific competitors (e.g., GoodRx, SingleCare, Cost Plus Drugs, pharmacy/insurer apps), include a comparison table, and explain why the niche focus plus budgeting is defensible and what stops GoodRx from copying it. Address that referral-based revenue creates an incentive conflict with 'unbiased' comparison and explain how trust will be maintained. (5) Validate the secondary markets and partnerships. Even 3-5 conversations or letters of interest from campus health centers, clinics, or one discount provider would substantially de-risk the plan. (6) Address regulatory, privacy and data risk concretely. Medication lists are sensitive health data; explain HIPAA applicability, data minimization, consent, security practices, and the licensing/reliability of price data, rather than deferring this to mentors. Also clarify how real-time pricing accuracy will be maintained, since wrong prices destroy trust. (7) Define a go-to-market and retention plan. Beyond campus outreach, explain acquisition channels, cost per user, and what drives ongoing use (refill reminders, budgeting) once a user finds their cheapest pharmacy, since the core value could be a one-time lookup. (8) Strengthen the team section. Highlight relevant domain experience, formalize advisors (pharmacist, health policy faculty), and identify gaps (health-data compliance, pharmacy partnerships). (9) Set explicit, measurable 12-month milestones tied to funding (e.g., 500 pilot users, $X average savings per user, 40% 60-day retention, one signed referral agreement). (10) Tighten structure: lead with a one-paragraph value proposition and key numbers, and consider adding a short roadmap and risk table so reviewers can see both ambition and evidence at a glance.
